note: The post says: 'When Rees purchased her property in 1888 for $15,000 from Mark Kimball, who lived next door at 2108 S. Prairie Avenue, Kimball's coach house extended across the back of both lots. It is believed that the Kimball house was built in the late 1860s, meaning that the coach house may actually pre-date the Great Chicago Fire (which bypassed the neighborhood). Rees acquired ownership of the south half of the coach house, and a party wall was constructed in the middle to divide it into two separate sections. The Kimball house and its half of the coach house were demolished in the 1930s, leaving the two-story Rees coach house intact.' It gives the surviving (Rees) half as 'The coach house measures 25 feet wide by 35 feet deep, stands 23 feet high, and weighs 187 tons', says it 'had a full basement', and that 'Story has it that the carriages utilized the ground floor, and a ramp was used to take the horses down to the stables in the basement level. The coachman would have occupied the rooms on the second story.' The photograph shows a two-storey common-brick building with level wall heads and no roof seen above them: a three-bay face with tall segmental-headed windows with keystones on the upper floor, and a long blank brick face.
what_it_supplies: one building across the alley ends of 2108 and 2110, divided by a party wall in the middle from 1888
the south (Rees) half's size in 2014: 25 ft wide, 35 ft deep, 23 ft high
the full basement and the ramp the horses went down to it; carriages on the ground floor, the coachman upstairs
the flat roof behind level wall heads, and the segmental-headed upper windows, as the building stood in 2014
what_it_does_not_supply: the north (Kimball) half, demolished in the 1930s
which face the photograph's three-bay front is, or where the carriage doors were
a date of building: 'may actually pre-date the Great Chicago Fire' is the post's belief
